IF the first question your Tech asks is "what brand", it is time to find another tech.

Why, if the next question is "what model"? Those are probably the first two questions I'd ask if someone called me for help -- partly because working on an extremely old machine is a waste of time and money for all concerned (unless it's for migrating data, that makes sense), and partly because some machines are notorious for not being amenable to third-party repairs (I'm looking at you, Apple). I'm not going to take on a job that isn't worth it. Either the client will be unhappy at the cost, or they'll try to screw me out of the money after the fact because "it's not worth it for that old thing".

I got tired of trying to maintain my mother's Compaq nc6220 despite the fact that I had recently installed a 160GB drive, and that it was (and still is) in perfect operating condition. It's just too damn slow and barely runs Windows 7 (because 915G chipset), so Windows 10 is right out. Even my netbook can run Windows 10! So I replaced it with something (Dell Inspiron 1525, hardly recent but at least "modern" in its standards) that actually has SATA and HDMI and a card reader that does more than 0.7MB/s. Sometimes it's better to just rule out machines like this up front, so I would ask.

Most support calls are due to software, not hardware. It is rare that a model number helps diagnose a problem, It may tell you that the device in question is very old, but asking the customer a model number is usually an unnecessary hassle, They will inadvertently give you the wrong number, or have difficulty finding it, despite clear instruction. More simple, direct questions work better, "what kind of issue are you having" "is this a pc or mac". This line of questioning leads to a diagnosis more quickly. It is rare that i come across a machine i cannot fix, and have gained many loyal customers over the years by fixing what i personally felt were antiquated systems, where the customer was told by other technicians that they must purchase a new unit, or that their machine wasn't "worth fixing". I usually tell the customer i am happy to transfer all their data if they wish to purchase a new machine, which i recommend, but that i will also repair their current machine if that is what they wish.

Disclaimer: i'm the kind of guy that kits out a hot air machine and large collection of components that live in the service vehicle. By carrying this, a few power supplies, disk drives, and fans, i can usually repair whatever it is on site, and not have to return.

I don't generally get software support calls, unless the problems are so severe that they cannot easily be distinguished from hardware problems by the user. If someone wants me to fix software, that's what Remote Desktop is for. If I actually have to take possession of a machine, it's almost always broken. That's when I'll apply the screening of "what make and model?" to make sure I'm not about to get a 10 year old laptop dumped in my lap that's not going to work significantly better when I'm done with it because it just can't (short of using a lighter-weight OS, but that's not what the user wants).

I've had it happen. I had a friend deliver his old laptop. First it was just freaking out in general, so I applied Memtest86, which revealed bad RAM. I swapped in some known good RAM, and it still tested bad. Turns out one of the two SODIMM slots was fried. I called him and made sure it was OK to buy a single SODIMM that maxed out the capacity of the one remaining slot, and he approved. Then I tried to get the networking to work. The damn thing was crawling with malware, and my attempts to connect to various places kept getting hijacked. I spent a couple hours chasing all of this down. I finally got it working as well as it was ever going to, and wrote up the invoice which came to $100 including the replacement part. I also returned all removed parts as the RAM was probably fine, it just wasn't useful for that particular situation.

His wife was PISSED that I would charge so much to fix an "old machine that isn't worth it". I agreed that he probably would have been better served spending the money on a new machine, but he still would have had to figure out how to get all of his data off of it. Not only did I never get a call to work on any of his computer equipment again, I stopped getting calls for other kinds of gigs too because the wife controlled the checkbook. Now I don't take the risk. I will decline machines that I do not believe are economically viable to work on, without even knowing what the problem is, because if I turn them down after inspection, I'm not even going to get paid for the inspection because I'm the one refusing the job.

It's not just age. If you have a seven year old netbook with a first-generation Atom, I'm going to decline the job. If you bring me a "real" laptop of the same age with a Core 2 Duo, I'm probably going to take the job. It's not that I hate the Atom netbook -- in fact I have one and still use it -- but 32-bit machines with a 2 (or 1.5) GB maximum RAM capacity are nearing end-of-life, and I don't want people feeling ripped off because they threw money at a machine they had to retire soon afterward. If they were to ask me how to extend the useful life of their netbook, I'd happily suggest getting an entry-level SSD (because the SATA I interface makes anything more a waste), and point them to Youtube videos on how to do the installation. But I wouldn't take the job.

I've also been burned doing work FOR FREE. I've replaced something at cost, then three months later when something else went out on the same machine, they blamed me and I had to fix it AGAIN at MY EXPENSE, or risk losing a contract with one of their family members. Now I don't take on that work either. (One exception: if I gave them that machine as a hand-me-down, I'll probably fix it because even if it does keel over later, it's hard to get mad at the guy who gave it to them for free in the first place.)
